unit.title: Reflexives & daily life
unit.subtitle: Your routine: levantarse, acostarse, vestirse, and 'each other'

grammar.title: Verbs that point back at you
grammar.intro: Your whole day is built on reflexive verbs — actions you do to yourself: you wake yourself up, wash yourself, dress yourself. In Spanish these carry a little pronoun (me, te, se, nos) that must never disappear. The infinitive ends in -se: levantarse, acostarse, vestirse.

sections.heading: The daily routine
sections.body: Put me before the verb for “I”, te for “you”, se for “he/she”. Some of these also change their stem (acostarse → me acuesto, vestirse → me visto):

ex.en: I go to bed at eleven.

sections.heading: Each other: nos vemos, se conocen
sections.body: With nosotros and ellos, the same pronoun can mean “each other”. Nos vemos = we see each other. Se conocen = they know each other.

ex.en: See you tomorrow. (We see each other.)
Ana and Luis know each other well.

sections.heading: Reflexives in the past
sections.body: In the preterite, keep the pronoun and change the ending: me levanté, me acosté, me vestí. The pronoun stays out front:

ex.en: Last night I went to bed at twelve.

takeaways: Reflexive pronouns: me, te, se, nos — never drop them.
Routine verbs: levantarse, ducharse, vestirse, acostarse, sentirse.
Stem changes: me acuesto, me visto.
nos/se can mean 'each other': nos vemos, se conocen.
Past keeps the pronoun: me levanté, me acosté.

mistakes.why: The reflexive pronoun 'me' is required — don't drop it.
acostarse is stem-changing: o → ue, so me acuesto.
If it's about you, use 'me', not 'te'. Match the pronoun to the subject.
